claims.text: Thermomechanically processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni forms a single-phase FCC alloy.
Composition variations in FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys alter local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions modulate the distribution of stacking fault energy.
Changes in stacking fault energy shift the dominant deformation mechanism between twinning and dislocation glide.
The balance between deformation twinning and dislocation glide governs mechanical-property differences among the quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys.
Elemental substitutions change atomic-size mismatches and local electronic environments.
Changes in atomic-size mismatch and electronic environment modify local lattice distortion and stacking fault energy.
Lower stacking fault energy favors deformation twinning and higher strain hardening.
Higher stacking fault energy favors conventional dislocation glide.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, modified alloys with lower effective stacking fault energy will exhibit more twinning and greater strain hardening.
The increased twinning and strain hardening predicted for lower-SFE alloys will produce higher yield strength.
Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, modified alloys with higher effective stacking fault energy will exhibit less twinning, more dislocation glide, and lower yield strength.
Secondary-phase formation or processing-induced changes in FCC stability may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Elemental clustering or segregation may significantly influence deformation behavior independently of stacking fault energy.
